questions.q: Why does parameterized querying solve SQL injection but have no direct equivalent for prompt injection?
options: Parameterized queries are actually vulnerable to the same style of attack as prompt injection
SQL injection was never a real vulnerability to begin with
LLMs do not accept any text input, so the comparison does not apply
SQL has a formal, bounded grammar that lets a database structurally separate command from value; natural language has no bounded grammar to parameterize against
questions.explain: Parameterized queries work because SQL's grammar is finite and enforceable. Natural language expresses the same intent in effectively unlimited phrasings, so there is no equivalent structural boundary to enforce.

questions.q: Why does keyword-based denylisting fail as a complete defense against prompt injection?
options: Keyword denylisting is actually a complete defense and no further layers are needed
The same intent can be paraphrased, translated, encoded, split across turns, or phrased as a hypothetical in effectively unlimited ways, so filtering meaning has no syntax checker to rely on
Denylisting only works on video content, not text
LLM providers block all denylisting attempts at the API level automatically
questions.explain: You are trying to filter meaning, not a bounded grammar — block one phrasing and semantically identical ones remain unblocked.

questions.q: What does this lesson say about delimiting or explicitly labeling untrusted content before it enters the prompt?
options: It is completely useless and should never be attempted
It is a mandatory legal requirement under the OWASP Top 10
It raises the bar and is worth doing, but it's a mitigation, not a guarantee — the model's adherence to the boundary is a matter of probability, not enforcement
It is a cryptographic technique that mathematically guarantees the model cannot be manipulated
questions.explain: Delimiting helps, but a sufficiently crafted injection can still attempt to talk its way out of the boundary — it is one layer among several, not a hard guarantee.

questions.q: According to this lesson, which approach actually holds up against prompt injection, given that there is no single input-side fix?
options: Defense in depth — output validation before action, least-privilege tool access, human-in-the-loop approval for consequential actions, monitoring, and red-teaming, layered together
Switching to a different programming language for the backend
Relying entirely on a single, sufficiently comprehensive keyword denylist
Disabling all logging so attackers cannot study the system's responses
questions.explain: Because no single filter can perfectly classify natural language, the weight shifts to multiple independent controls so no one failure point compromises the whole system.

questions.q: Where does input sanitization actually belong in a real defensive strategy against prompt injection, per this lesson?
options: It should be removed entirely since it provides zero value
As one reasonable first layer that filters out the laziest attempts — but treating it as sufficient on its own is itself the vulnerability
It should be the only layer of defense, since it already stops all injection attempts
It is illegal to filter user input under current AI regulation
questions.explain: Sanitization still has a place in the layered defense; the mistake is treating it as the whole defense rather than one layer among several.
